clue.text: About to go back to a security organisation — one with several branches

indicators.note: going back means the letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: CA, short for circa, means about
taken as written
the American Central Intelligence Agency

explanation.surface: Someone is about to return to a security agency that has many regional branches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Branches' looks like offices of the organisation, but it is the tree's limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: An acacia is a tree, and a tree is a thing with many branches.

clue.text: Painting Caruso performing with choir

indicators.note: performing suggests the letters are put through their paces and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A picture of the tenor Enrico Caruso singing alongside a choir.
explanation.definitionFit: Chiaroscuro is the painting technique of strong contrast between light and shade, so it names a style of painting.

clue.text: Class left out of big house

indicators.note: out of says the named letter is taken away from the word that follows

parts.note: a castle is a very large house
L is the usual abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone of a certain class has been excluded from the grand house.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the L from CASTLE to leave CASTE.
explanation.definitionFit: A caste is a hereditary social class, especially in the Hindu system.

clue.text: A jolly cleaner goes round one piece of furniture

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: taken as written
a Jolly is slang for a Royal Marine, RM
a char or charwoman is a cleaning lady
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A cheerful cleaner dusts around a single item of furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' looks like an adjective for the cleaner, but it is the noun for a Royal Marine; CHAR wraps I to make CHAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: An armchair is a comfortable chair with arm supports, a standard piece of furniture.

clue.text: Old head has a gin, say, after school

indicators.note: after places the following piece behind the one named next

parts.note: S is an abbreviation for school, as in LSE
taken as written
a gin is a kind of snare, an example of a trap

explanation.surface: A former headmaster enjoys a gin once school is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gin' looks like the drink, but it is the gin trap used to catch animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A satrap was a provincial governor in ancient Persia, so a ruler or head from olden times.

clue.text: Back in a short while

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to support a proposal formally
a moment, as in 'just a sec'

explanation.surface: Someone promises to return very soon.
explanation.definitionFit: To second a motion is to back it, and a second is a very brief moment of time.

clue.text: Swimming manager fills dry bag

indicators.note: something swimming moves about loosely, so these letters drift into a new order
filling something means going inside it

parts.note: TT means teetotal, someone who stays off drink
the letters rearranged to sit between the two Ts

explanation.surface: A manager in the pool stuffs things into a dry bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bag' looks like a container but is the insulting word for an unpleasant old woman; 'dry bag' reads as a waterproof sack.
explanation.definitionFit: A termagant is a scolding, overbearing woman, and old bag is a derogatory term for one.

clue.text: Grog makes you dim when put under pressure

indicators.note: the answer becomes the other word once the pressure symbol sits above it, so the answer is that word minus the symbol

parts.note: pale means faint or dim in colour
P is the symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: Drinking grog dulls your wits once you are put under strain.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay works backwards: put P above the answer in this down clue and it becomes PALE, meaning dim.
explanation.definitionFit: Grog is loosely any alcoholic drink, and ale is beer, so one example of it.

clue.text: Farm facility with fallen leader, grabbed by criminal mastermind with yen for dodgy deals

indicators.note: being grabbed means being held inside something else
a leader that has fallen drops from the front of the word to the bottom, which in a down clue is the end

parts.note: the Joker is Batman's criminal mastermind enemy
a piggery is a pig farm building
Y is the abbreviation for the Japanese yen

explanation.surface: A criminal kingpin with a taste for shady business takes over a pig unit whose boss has been toppled.
explanation.walkthrough: The leader is not lost but falls: in a down entry the first letter drops to the foot of the word. The Joker is the Batman villain.
explanation.definitionFit: Jiggery-pokery is informal for underhand scheming or trickery, which is what dodgy deals are.

clue.text: One can't go off at nights

definitions.text: One can't go off at nights

parts.words: One can't go off at nights
parts.note: surface reading: someone who is not allowed to go out in the evening
setter's reading: to drop off, to fall asleep, which this person cannot do at night

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go off' suggests leaving the house; here it means nodding off.
explanation.definitionFit: An insomniac is a person who habitually cannot fall asleep at night.

clue.text: Perth perv returned to dance

indicators.note: returned means turned back, so the word is read from the end

parts.note: in Australian slang, as spoken in Perth, to perv is to ogle or leer

explanation.surface: A lecherous man from Perth comes back to a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perth' tells you the slang is Australian, where 'perv' as a verb means to look lustfully.
explanation.definitionFit: A reel is a lively Scottish or Irish folk dance.

clue.text: Seat in tree is rare

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: the beech is a tree
R is an abbreviation for rare

explanation.surface: A seat built up in a tree is an unusual sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat' means the backside here, not a chair; R goes after the B of BEECH.
explanation.definitionFit: Breech is an old word for the buttocks, and seat is another word for the same part of the body.

clue.text: French policeman or criminal armed with information

indicators.note: criminal suggests something bent or crooked, so the letters are twisted out of order

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Is this French officer a cop, or a crook carrying a gun and some intelligence?
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' joins the anagram to GEN, which is placed first.
explanation.definitionFit: A gendarme is a member of the French armed police force.

clue.text: To defeat hunk is an outstanding achievement

parts.note: to master is to overcome or defeat
a hunk is a big piece of something

explanation.surface: Beating a handsome man is a fine accomplishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hunk' suggests an attractive man; here it is a chunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A masterpiece is a work of supreme skill, an outstanding achievement.

clue.text: Train Earl to get more canny touring Pennsylvania

parts.note: E is an abbreviation for earl

indicators.note: touring a place means travelling around it, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: slier means more sly or crafty
PA is the postal code for Pennsylvania

explanation.surface: An aristocrat takes a train to become shrewder while travelling through Pennsylvania.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' looks like a railway noun, but it is the verb for guiding a plant's growth.
explanation.definitionFit: To espalier a fruit tree is to train its branches flat against a wall or frame.

clue.text: American left a flashing light outside as a navigator's aid

indicators.note: being outside something means wrapping round it

parts.note: A is a common abbreviation for American
a strobe is a light that flashes rapidly
L is the usual abbreviation for left
taken as written

explanation.surface: An American abandoned a flashing beacon outside to help guide sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the past tense of leave; it is just L. STROBE wraps L and A.
explanation.definitionFit: An astrolabe was an instrument used by early navigators to measure the altitude of stars.

clue.text: Monkey outside small recess

indicators.note: being outside something means wrapping round it

parts.note: an ape is a primate like a monkey
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A monkey sits outside a little alcove.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is a semicircular recess, typically at the east end of a church.

clue.text: Stupid angler almost hit pipe

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
stupid suggests something muddled, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
the word with its last letter removed

explanation.surface: A foolish fisherman nearly struck a pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stupid' looks like an insult to the angler, but it signals the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A narghile is an oriental water pipe for smoking tobacco, also called a hookah.

clue.text: Ruined a sculpture

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a sculpted head and shoulders

explanation.surface: Someone has smashed a statue.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bust is broken or wrecked, and a bust is a carved likeness of the head and chest.

clue.text: During psalm conductor talks foolishly

indicators.note: during means in the middle of, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: Ps is the abbreviation for Psalm, as in Bible references
Sir Simon Rattle is a famous British orchestral conductor

explanation.surface: A conductor chatters nonsense in the middle of a psalm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' might suggest a bus or electrical one, but it is the musician Simon Rattle.
explanation.definitionFit: To prattle is to chatter in a silly or childish way.

clue.text: Blackpool is known for such organs

definitions.text: Blackpool is known for such organs

parts.note: the seaside resort of Blackpool in north-west England is famous for its autumn Illuminations
setter's reading: animal lungs, which butchers call by this same word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Organs' suggests Blackpool Tower's famous Wurlitzer, but it means lungs; Blackpool's Illuminations are a long seafront display of electric bulbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Lights is the traditional butcher's term for the lungs of a slaughtered animal, and the word also names the resort's famous displays.

clue.text: Robert put old tie on American bird

indicators.note: put signals the pieces are placed one after another in sequence

parts.note: Bob is a short form of Robert
O is an abbreviation for old
to tie is to link

explanation.surface: Robert wears an old necktie featuring an American bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The bobolink is a North American songbird of the blackbird family.

clue.text: Doctor entertains artist with piano and a brandy

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so one piece holds the others

parts.note: a GP is a general practitioner, a family doctor
RA is a Royal Academician
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
taken as written

explanation.surface: A doctor hosts a painter with a piano and offers a brandy.
explanation.definitionFit: Grappa is an Italian brandy distilled from grape residue left after winemaking.

clue.text: Quickly take horse from native American

indicators.note: take something from a word means remove it from that word

parts.note: the Apache are a Native American people
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: Hurry and seize a horse from a Native American rider.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse' is drug slang for heroin, H.
explanation.definitionFit: Apace is a literary word meaning swiftly or at speed.

clue.text: Bats finally settling on stove

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word

parts.note: the final letter of the word
an Aga is a British brand of range cooker

explanation.surface: Bats eventually come to roost on top of a stove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' looks like the flying animals, but it is slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Bats and gaga are both informal words for mad or senile.

clue.text: Bother sandboy, now and then

indicators.note: now and then means only occasionally, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A cheery sandboy occasionally gets annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happy as a sandboy' is a British saying for being carefree.
explanation.definitionFit: Ado means fuss or trouble, as in much ado about nothing, so it is bother.

clue.text: Short belt — one form of punishment creating a storm!

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to belt is to hurry, here missing its last letter
the Roman numeral for one
the cane was used to beat schoolchildren

explanation.surface: A brief strapping and a beating cause an uproar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belt' suggests a leather strap or a blow; here it is the verb meaning to rush.
explanation.definitionFit: A hurricane is a violent tropical storm with very strong winds.

clue.text: Great cricketer becomes more like a judge?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Sir Garfield ..., the great West Indian all-rounder
second meaning: grows more sober, from the saying 'sober as a judge'

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading via the idiom 'sober as a judge'.
explanation.definitionFit: Garry Sobers was a celebrated cricketer, and someone who sobers up becomes as sober as the proverbial judge.

clue.text: Flat behind the Spanish cardinal

indicators.note: behind places one piece after the other in sequence

parts.note: el is Spanish for the
flat ground is even

explanation.surface: A level spot lies behind the Spanish churchman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal' suggests a churchman, but it means a cardinal number.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleven is a cardinal number, one used for counting rather than ordering.
